title: Robinson Admissible Sequence Lemma
body_html:
Robinson Admissible Sequence Lemma

Setup

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be a matrix-game payoff. Write $\|A\| := \max_{i,j}|A_{i,j}|$.

For $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^m$ define $$ J(\alpha) := \{j : \alpha^j = \min_k \alpha^k\}, \qquad I(\beta) := \{i : \beta^i = \max_k \beta^k\}. $$

An admissible sequence is $(\alpha(t), \beta(t))_{t \ge 0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m$ satisfying

  • (i) $\min_k \alpha^k(0) = \max_k \beta^k(0)$;
  • (ii) at each $t \ge 0$, $\exists i_{t+1} \in I(\beta(t))$, $j_{t+1} \in J(\alpha(t))$ with $$ \alpha(t+1) = \alpha(t) + e_{i_{t+1}}^T A, \qquad \beta(t+1) = \beta(t) + A e_{j_{t+1}}. $$

This is a cumulative-payoff encoding of fictitious play ([[zero_sum.fictitious_play.fictitious_play]]): writing $x(t) := \frac1t \sum_{s \le t} e_{i_s}$ and $y(t) := \frac1t \sum_{s \le t} e_{j_s}$ for the empirical frequencies, $$ \frac{\alpha(t) - \alpha(0)}{t} = x(t) A, \qquad \frac{\beta(t) - \beta(0)}{t} = A y(t). $$

The central quantity is the cumulative duality gap $$ \mu(t) := \max_i \beta^i(t) - \min_j \alpha^j(t). $$

Statement

Lemma (Robinson 1951). For every matrix $A$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $s_0 = s_0(A, \varepsilon)$ such that $$ \mu(t) \le \varepsilon \cdot t, \quad \forall t \ge s_0, $$ for every admissible sequence on $A$.

Equivalently, $\mu(t) = o(t)$, uniformly over admissible sequences.
proof_html:
structure

By induction on the matrix size $N := m + n$.

Base $N = 2$ (i.e., $1 \times 1$ matrix): $\mu(t) = 0$. Trivial.

Inductive step assumes the lemma for every strict submatrix of $A$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$:

  1. Hypothesis transport. By induction, for every strict submatrix $A'$ there exists $s(A', \varepsilon / 2)$ bounding $\mu'(t) \le (\varepsilon/2) t$ on admissible sequences of $A'$. There are finitely many such submatrices, so $$ t^* := \max_{A' \subseteq A} s(A', \varepsilon/2) $$ is finite.

  2. Window dichotomy. Fix any $s$ and look at the window $[s, s + t^*]$. Two mutually exclusive cases:

  3. All rows and columns useful in the window. By [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.robinson_admissible_lemma.useful_window]], $$ \mu(s + t^*) \le 4 t^* \|A\| $$ — an absolute bound that resets $\mu$ regardless of its value at $s$.

  4. Some row $i$ or column $j$ is not useful in the window. By [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.robinson_admissible_lemma.subgame_reduction]], the window is governed by admissible play on a strict submatrix; the inductive hypothesis then gives $$ \mu(s + t^*) - \mu(s) \le \frac{\varepsilon t^*}{2} + 2\|A\|. $$

  5. Pasting. Decompose $t = q t^* + r$ with $0 \le r < t^*$ and apply the dichotomy to consecutive windows. By [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.robinson_admissible_lemma.induction_step]], $$ \mu(t) \;\le\; 6 t^* \|A\| + \frac{\varepsilon t}{2} + \frac{2\|A\| t}{t^*}. $$

  6. Constant selection. Replacing $t^*$ by $\max(t^*, 4\|A\|/\varepsilon)$ (still a valid bound from the inductive hypothesis), the last term is bounded by $\varepsilon t / 2$. Choosing $s_0 := \max(t^*, 12 t^* \|A\| / \varepsilon)$ then yields $\mu(t) \le \frac{3\varepsilon}{2} t$ for $t \ge s_0$. Re-running the argument with $\varepsilon / 2$ gives the stated bound $\mu(t) \le \varepsilon t$.

The bracketing invariant [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.robinson_admissible_lemma.bracket_invariant]] (namely $\min_i \beta^i(s) \le \max_j \alpha^j(s)$ for every admissible $s$) is used inside the useful-window estimate. $\square$

Consequence

Combined with the trivial bracket $\min_j x(t)Ay \le \underline v(A) \le \overline v(A) \le \max_i x(t) A^i$, the lemma yields the existence of a value $v(A) = \underline v = \overline v$ and gives that every accumulation point of $(x(t), y(t))$ is an optimal-strategy pair. This is the content of [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.fictitious_play_convergence]].

For the Cesàro average payoff statement $\frac1n \sum_{p \le n} A_{i_p, j_p} \to v$, see the independent telescoping argument in [[zero_sum.fictitious_play.cesaro_payoff_from_robinson]].

References

  • [Robinson 1951] J. Robinson, "An iterative method of solving a game", Annals of Mathematics 54 (1951), 296–301.
  • [MFoGT, Section 2.8, Exercise 12] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory, references/MathFoundationsGameTheory.pdf. Hint-decomposition of Robinson's proof into the four internal lemmas cited above.
